name: Grilled Chicken Thighs with Tabbouleh, Hummus & Turmeric Rice

elevations.title: Yogurt-Spice Marinade, 4 Hours Minimum
elevations.instruction: Mix 1 cup full-fat plain yogurt with 2 crushed garlic cloves, 1 teaspoon cumin, 1 teaspoon coriander, 1/2 teaspoon smoked paprika, the juice of one lemon, 2 tablespoons olive oil, and a generous pinch of salt. Coat bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and refrigerate for at least 4 hours — overnight is better. The yogurt does two jobs: its lactic acid tenderizes the meat while its proteins create a caramelized crust on the grill that you cannot replicate with oil-based marinades. Pat the skin side dry with a paper towel before grilling so it crisps instead of steams.
elevations.why: Yogurt marinades are the reason Turkish and Lebanese grilled meats taste different from American backyard chicken. The casein proteins in yogurt brown aggressively on a hot grill, creating a crust that's both charred and impossibly juicy underneath. Four hours minimum — anything less and you're just coating, not marinating.

elevations.title: Bloom the Turmeric in Fat Before It Touches the Rice
elevations.instruction: Heat 2 tablespoons of butter or olive oil in your pot until it shimmers. Add 1 teaspoon ground turmeric, 1/2 teaspoon cumin, and 3 cracked cardamom pods. Stir for 60 seconds until the oil turns deep gold and smells like a spice market, not a spice jar. Add your rinsed basmati rice and toast it in this bloomed spice fat for 2 minutes, stirring to coat every grain, before adding your stock. Finish the cooked rice with a handful of toasted slivered almonds and a scattering of golden raisins.
elevations.why: Raw turmeric stirred into cooking liquid tastes like dirt. Turmeric bloomed in hot fat releases curcumin — its fat-soluble flavor compound — and transforms from earthy and flat to warm, peppery, and almost floral. The toasted rice grains stay separate and fluffy instead of clumping.

elevations.title: Board Sauce for the Chicken
elevations.instruction: While the chicken rests (5 minutes, tented loosely — never tightly — with foil), build a board sauce: on a large cutting board, mince together 1/4 cup flat-leaf parsley, 2 tablespoons fresh mint, 1 crushed garlic clove, and the zest of one lemon. Spread this herb paste across the board. Add a generous thread of your best olive oil, a pinch of flaky salt, and a crack of black pepper. Slice the rested chicken directly on top of this herb carpet so every slice picks up bright, raw flavor on its underside.
elevations.why: A board sauce is a finishing technique that delivers raw herb intensity that cooking would destroy. The warm chicken juices melt into the herbs and oil, creating an instant pan sauce without a pan. It's the single best zero-effort upgrade for any grilled protein.

elevations.title: Hand-Chop the Tabbouleh — Never Pulse
elevations.instruction: Chop your flat-leaf parsley and mint by hand with a sharp chef's knife — never a food processor. You want clean cuts, not bruised mush. Use a 5:1 ratio of parsley to bulgur. Soak fine bulgur in cold water for only 15 minutes, then squeeze it bone-dry in a kitchen towel before adding to the herbs. Dress with equal parts lemon juice and olive oil, a diced garden tomato, and fine-diced cucumber. Season aggressively with salt — tabbouleh that tastes flat is always under-seasoned.
elevations.why: A food processor ruptures cell walls and turns parsley into a wet green paste. Hand-chopping preserves the herb's structure and bright, grassy flavor. Authentic tabbouleh is an herb salad with a whisper of grain, not a grain salad with herbs — the ratio is everything.

name: Corned Beef Hash with Fried Eggs & Toast

elevations.title: The Cast-Iron Crust Protocol
elevations.instruction: Dice your potatoes into 1/4-inch cubes, parboil for exactly 6 minutes until fork-tender but not falling apart, then spread on a sheet pan and refrigerate until completely cold — 30 minutes minimum, or use last night's leftovers. Heat your cast-iron skillet screaming hot with 2 tablespoons of butter. Add the cold potatoes in a single layer, press down firmly with a spatula, and do not touch them for 4 full minutes. You'll hear aggressive sizzling — that's the Maillard reaction earning you a golden crust. Flip in sections, add your diced corned beef, press again, and give it another 3 minutes undisturbed.
elevations.why: Cold, dry potatoes + screaming hot fat + patience = a hash with a shatteringly crisp exterior and creamy interior. Every time you stir, you reset the crust clock to zero. The cast-iron's heat retention means the temperature doesn't crash when food hits the pan — stainless and nonstick can't compete here.

elevations.title: Smoked Paprika Butter Baste
elevations.instruction: In the last 2 minutes of cooking, add 1 tablespoon of butter, 1/2 teaspoon of smoked paprika, and a few dashes of Worcestershire sauce to the hash. Tilt the pan and spoon the melting, red-tinted butter over the hash repeatedly for 60 seconds. The paprika blooms in the hot butter and the Worcestershire adds umami depth that makes this taste like a diner that's been open since 1947.
elevations.why: Smoked paprika and butter is the world's cheapest flavor amplifier. The paprika's fat-soluble pigments dissolve into the butter, coating every surface with smoky, sweet warmth. The Worcestershire adds fermented anchovy umami that you'll never identify but absolutely miss if it's gone.

elevations.title: Crispy-Edged Fried Eggs with Olive Oil
elevations.instruction: Forget butter for the eggs tonight. Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a nonstick pan over medium-high heat until the oil shimmers and a drop of water sizzles on contact. Crack your eggs directly in — the whites will bubble and fry, creating lacy, crispy brown edges while the yolk stays molten. Tilt the pan and spoon hot oil over the yolk whites to set the top without flipping. Season with flaky salt and a crack of pepper. Total time: 90 seconds. The yolk should run when you break it with toast — that's the sauce for your hash.
elevations.why: Olive oil gets hotter than butter without burning, which means crispier edges. The oil baste sets the top of the egg without the violence of flipping. A runny yolk is not optional — it's the only sauce this dish needs, and it ties the salty hash to the crunchy toast in every bite.

name: Babo Pasta — Homemade Spinach Pasta with Egg Yolks

elevations.title: Cacio e Uovo: The Egg-Yolk Emulsion
elevations.instruction: In a bowl, whisk together 3 egg yolks and 1 cup of finely grated Pecorino Romano until it forms a thick paste. Add 2 tablespoons of starchy pasta water — reserved before draining — and whisk until it's the consistency of heavy cream. Pull your cooked pasta off the heat, wait 30 seconds for the pan to cool slightly, then pour the egg-cheese mixture over the hot pasta and toss vigorously for 60 seconds. The residual heat emulsifies the eggs into a silky, glossy cream that clings to every strand. If it looks dry, add more pasta water one tablespoon at a time. If it scrambles, your pan was too hot — start again.
elevations.why: Last week you did brown butter and sage — this week we lean into the egg yolks that make Babo Pasta special. This is essentially the cacio e pepe technique applied to your spinach pasta, and it turns the egg yolks from a structural ingredient into the star of the sauce. The starchy pasta water is the emulsifier that keeps everything creamy instead of clumpy.

elevations.title: Crispy Garlic-Breadcrumb Pangritata
elevations.instruction: Tear 2 slices of day-old bread into rough crumbs (or pulse once in a food processor — you want irregular pieces, not dust). In a skillet over medium heat, warm 3 tablespoons of olive oil and add 2 thinly sliced garlic cloves. The moment the garlic turns pale gold — 90 seconds, watch it — add the breadcrumbs, a pinch of red pepper flakes, and a pinch of salt. Toss constantly for 3-4 minutes until the crumbs are deeply golden and crunchy. Scatter generously over each bowl of pasta.
elevations.why: Pangritata is called 'the poor man's Parmesan' in southern Italy, and it solves the one problem fresh pasta always has: textural monotony. Soft, silky noodles need something to interrupt the smoothness. These garlic-perfumed, crunchy crumbs do what toasted pine nuts did last week, but with a completely different flavor profile — more rustic, more assertive.

elevations.title: The Pasta Water Protocol
elevations.instruction: Before you drain the pasta, ladle out a full 2 cups of the starchy cooking water into a heat-safe measuring cup. This is not optional — this water is liquid gold. It contains dissolved starch from your fresh pasta that acts as a natural emulsifier. When you combine it with fat (butter, oil, egg yolks, cheese), it creates a silky sauce that clings instead of pools. Add it 1-2 tablespoons at a time while tossing the pasta in its sauce. The final dish should look glossy and slightly wet — it will tighten as it cools on the plate.
elevations.why: Professional Italian cooks finish every pasta in its sauce with pasta water. Home cooks drain and dump. This single habit is the difference between pasta that tastes like it came from a restaurant and pasta that tastes like Tuesday night. The starch concentration from fresh pasta is even higher than dried, making your pasta water an even more powerful tool.

elevations.title: Sharp Fennel-Lemon Side Salad
elevations.instruction: Shave half a fennel bulb paper-thin on a mandoline (use the guard — I mean it). Toss with the juice of half a lemon, 1 tablespoon of olive oil, a pinch of flaky salt, and a few shavings of Parmigiano-Reggiano. Let it sit for 10 minutes — the acid softens the fennel's crunch just enough while keeping its anise brightness. Serve alongside the pasta in a separate small bowl. A forkful between bites resets your palate from the richness of the egg-cheese sauce.
elevations.why: Rich, egg-yolk pasta with a cheese sauce needs a sharp, cold counterpoint or your palate goes numb by the fourth bite. Raw fennel with lemon is the Italian tradition for cutting through richness — the anise flavor bridges the herbal notes in the spinach pasta while the acid lifts everything. This is not a salad course; it's a palate tool.

name: Lemon Ricotta Pancakes with Berry Compote

elevations.title: Whip the Whites Separately — This Is a Soufflé, Not a Flapjack
elevations.instruction: Separate your eggs. Mix the yolks into the wet ingredients with the ricotta, lemon zest, and lemon juice. In a separate clean bowl, whip the egg whites to medium-soft peaks — they should hold their shape but still have a slight droop at the tip. Fold the whites into the batter in two additions: the first stir can be aggressive to lighten the batter, the second fold must be gentle — use a spatula, lift from the bottom, fold over the top, rotate the bowl, repeat until just barely incorporated. You'll see white streaks. That's correct. Those streaks are air, and air is what makes these pancakes three-dimensional.
elevations.why: Whipped whites are the difference between a dense ricotta pancake and one that rises like a cloud. The air trapped in the meringue expands on the griddle, creating an interior that's almost custard-like. Overmixing deflates the whites and you're back to regular pancakes. This technique is borrowed from soufflé making — it works here for the same physics.

elevations.title: Blistered Berry Compote with Balsamic and Black Pepper
elevations.instruction: Combine 2 cups of mixed berries (blueberries, raspberries, halved strawberries) with 2 tablespoons of sugar and 1 tablespoon of balsamic vinegar in a saucepan over medium heat. Cook until the berries begin to burst and release juice — about 5 minutes. Do not stir more than twice; you want some berries intact and some collapsed into sauce. Add a small pinch of black pepper and the zest of half a lemon at the very end. Remove from heat immediately. The compote should be loose, not jammy — it will thicken as it cools.
elevations.why: Balsamic vinegar and black pepper in berry compote is the restaurant move that nobody expects at breakfast-for-dinner. The vinegar deepens the berry flavor the way a squeeze of lemon does, but with more complexity and a whisper of aged sweetness. The pepper adds a warm finish that makes your tongue pay attention. This compote doesn't just taste sweet — it tastes interesting.

elevations.title: Honeyed Ricotta Quenelle
elevations.instruction: Mix 1/2 cup of fresh whole-milk ricotta with 1 tablespoon of honey, the zest of half a lemon, and a tiny pinch of salt. Keep it cold. When plating, use two spoons to form a quenelle — scoop a spoonful with one spoon, then use the second to shape it into a smooth football by passing it back and forth 3 times. Place the cold quenelle on top of the hot pancake stack. The contrast of cold, tangy, honey-sweet ricotta melting slowly over warm pancakes is a textural and temperature experience that elevates this from 'pancakes for dinner' to 'the pancakes we talk about all week.'
elevations.why: A cold element on a hot dish forces your palate to process two temperatures simultaneously, which heightens flavor perception. The honeyed ricotta also adds a protein-rich richness that balances the fruit acidity and makes these pancakes feel like a composed dessert, not just breakfast at 6 PM.

name: Chicken & Charred Corn Street Tacos with Elote Crema

elevations.title: Cumin-Lime Dry Brine, 2 Hours Ahead
elevations.instruction: Two hours before cooking, pat boneless, skinless chicken thighs dry and season generously on both sides with: 1 teaspoon salt, 1/2 teaspoon cumin, 1/2 teaspoon chili powder, 1/4 teaspoon garlic powder, the zest of one lime, and a crack of black pepper. Place uncovered on a plate in the refrigerator. The surface will dry out and the salt will penetrate — both of which are exactly what you want. When you sear this chicken in a screaming hot pan, the dry surface will brown instantly and the seasoning will have become part of the meat, not a coating that falls off.
elevations.why: A dry brine draws moisture to the surface, dissolves the salt, and then the brine reabsorbs into the meat through osmosis. In 2 hours, you get seasoning all the way through — not just on top. The dry surface creates better Maillard browning because moisture is the enemy of crust.

elevations.title: Char the Corn in a Dry Cast-Iron Pan
elevations.instruction: Cut corn kernels off 3 ears (or use frozen, thawed and patted very dry). Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with no oil until a drop of water vaporizes on contact. Add the corn kernels in a single layer — they will pop and spit, that's correct. Do not stir for 3 full minutes. You want blackened spots on at least half the kernels. Toss once, then leave for another 2 minutes. Hit the charred corn with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt right off the heat.
elevations.why: Dry-charring in cast iron mimics the intensity of an open grill or comal. Without oil, the kernels' natural sugars caramelize directly against the metal, creating blistered, smoky-sweet pops of flavor. Oil prevents this direct contact — dry is the move for corn.

elevations.title: Proper Elote Crema with Cotija and Smoked Chili
elevations.instruction: Stir together 1/4 cup Mexican crema (or sour cream), 2 tablespoons mayonnaise, 1/4 cup crumbled cotija cheese, the juice of 1 lime, 1/2 teaspoon chili powder, and a pinch of cayenne. Let it sit for 15 minutes so the cotija softens and the flavors marry. Thin with a splash of lime juice if needed — it should be drizzle-able, not spackle-thick. When plating, use a spoon to streak the crema across each taco in a zig-zag. Then crumble extra cotija over the top like snow.
elevations.why: Authentic elote dressing is the trinity of fat (mayo + crema), salt (cotija), and acid (lime). The smoked chili adds warmth without overwhelming Elsie's palate. Cotija is the secret — it's salty, crumbly, and doesn't melt, so it maintains texture in the finished taco instead of disappearing into the sauce.

elevations.title: Charred Tortillas and Quick-Pickled Red Onion
elevations.instruction: Slice half a red onion into paper-thin rings. Submerge in 1/3 cup lime juice, 1 teaspoon sugar, and 1/2 teaspoon salt. Let sit 20 minutes — they'll turn a screaming magenta. For the tortillas: hold each small flour tortilla directly over a gas burner with tongs for 10-15 seconds per side until you see black char spots and the tortilla puffs. If electric, use a bone-dry cast-iron pan at maximum heat. Wrap charred tortillas in a clean towel. The pickled onions go on last, right before the first bite — their acid cuts through every rich element on the taco.
elevations.why: Straight-from-the-bag room-temperature tortillas are an insult to everything inside them. Charring adds smoky bitterness that complements the elote crema. The quick-pickled onions provide the acid backbone that every taco needs — without them, it's just chicken and cheese in a wrapper.

elevations.title: Ricotta-Lemon-Herb Filling with Nutmeg
elevations.instruction: Drain 1 1/2 cups of whole-milk ricotta in cheesecloth for 30 minutes — squeeze out every drop of whey. Mix with 1/2 cup finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano, 1 egg yolk (not the whole egg — yolk only for richness without dilution), 2 tablespoons chopped fresh basil, 1 tablespoon chopped fresh chives, the zest of one lemon, a generous grating of fresh nutmeg (10 passes on a Microplane, no more), and salt and black pepper. Chill the filling for 30 minutes before assembling — cold filling holds its shape and makes sealing the ravioli dramatically easier.
elevations.why: Draining the ricotta is the step most home cooks skip, and it's the step that determines whether your ravioli are creamy pillows or soggy water balloons. The lemon zest and nutmeg are traditional Italian companions to ricotta that add warmth and brightness without competing. A chilled filling piped into the pasta is how restaurants maintain uniform, leak-proof ravioli.

elevations.title: Brown Butter with Crispy Sage and Toasted Hazelnuts
elevations.instruction: This is a date night, so we're doing the brown butter right. Cut 8 tablespoons of unsalted butter into a light-colored stainless steel pan. Cook over medium heat, swirling, until the milk solids on the bottom turn the color of a hazelnut shell and your kitchen smells like a Parisian bakery — 5 minutes, not a second longer. Drop in 15 fresh sage leaves — they'll sputter and crisp in 10 seconds. Add 3 tablespoons of roughly chopped toasted hazelnuts and 1 tablespoon of the ravioli cooking water. Swirl to emulsify. Gently nestle the drained ravioli into this pan and spoon the sauce over each one. Plate 5-6 per person — leave space on the plate.
elevations.why: Brown butter and sage with ricotta ravioli is not just a pairing — it's a canonical Italian dish that has survived centuries because it is perfect. The hazelnuts echo the toasted milk solids in the butter and add a crunch that plays against the soft, yielding ravioli. On a date night, less on the plate is more — each bite should be deliberate and savored.

elevations.title: Make the Pasta Together — It's the Date
elevations.instruction: Set up a pasta station at the counter with two glasses of wine. One person rolls the sheets through the pasta machine while the other fills and seals the ravioli. Make the dough with 2 cups of 00 flour and 6 egg yolks (no whites — all yolk makes an impossibly rich, golden dough for a special night). Knead 10 minutes, rest 30 minutes wrapped in plastic. Roll to the second-thinnest setting — you should almost see your hand through it. Seal each ravioli with a fork after pressing out the air. Count on 30 ravioli — 12-15 per person.
elevations.why: Homemade pasta is the most romantic cooking project in existence. It's tactile, collaborative, and produces something you simply cannot buy. The all-yolk dough is richer and silkier than a whole-egg dough — it's the special-occasion version that Italian grandmothers reserve for Sundays and celebrations. The imperfections in hand-made ravioli are features, not flaws.

elevations.title: Shaved Parmigiano and Lemon Zest at the Table
elevations.instruction: Bring a hunk of aged Parmigiano-Reggiano and a vegetable peeler to the table. Shave 4-5 wide curls over each plate right before eating. Follow with a generous crack of black pepper and the zest of half a lemon Microplaned directly over the dish from 6 inches up, so it falls like snow. Open a bottle of something cold and crisp — a Vermentino or a Gavi di Gavi. Light a candle. You earned this.
elevations.why: Tableside finishing turns dinner into an experience. The Parmigiano shavings melt slowly on the hot ravioli, releasing a different flavor profile than grated cheese mixed in. The pepper's volatile oils bloom when freshly cracked. The lemon zest — the final spark that prevents richness from becoming monotony. This is date night. Presentation matters.

name: Udon Soup with Premade Soup Dumplings

elevations.title: Build a Proper Dashi Broth from Scratch
elevations.instruction: Soak a 4-inch piece of kombu (dried kelp) in 6 cups of cold water for 30 minutes — patience, not heat, extracts its glutamates. Bring the pot slowly to just below a boil — you'll see tiny bubbles climbing the kombu but the surface isn't rolling. Pull the kombu out immediately (boiling it turns the broth bitter and slimy). Add a generous fistful of katsuobushi (bonito flakes), let them sink for 2 minutes, then strain through a fine-mesh sieve. Season this golden dashi with 3 tablespoons of soy sauce, 2 tablespoons of mirin, and 1 tablespoon of sake. Taste. Adjust. The broth should be clean, deeply savory, and slightly sweet.
elevations.why: Premade dumplings are fine — premade broth is a crime. Dashi takes 40 minutes including soaking and produces a broth with an umami depth that no carton or cube can replicate. Kombu contains natural glutamic acid and bonito adds inosinic acid — together they create a synergistic umami that's greater than the sum of its parts.

elevations.title: Crispy-Bottomed Dumplings — Pan-Fry First, Then Soup
elevations.instruction: Don't just drop the premade dumplings into the broth — that makes them waterlogged and indistinguishable from the noodles. Instead, heat 1 tablespoon of sesame oil in a nonstick pan over medium-high heat. Place dumplings flat-side down and cook undisturbed for 3 minutes until the bottoms are deeply golden and crispy. Add 1/4 cup of water, cover immediately, and steam for 4 minutes until cooked through. Nestle 3-4 crispy-bottomed dumplings into each bowl on top of the noodles, crispy side up, so the bottoms stay crunchy above the broth line.
elevations.why: Texture evolution within a single bowl is what separates a great soup from hot water with things in it. The crispy bottoms resist the broth long enough to give you 3-4 bites of contrast, then gradually yield to the liquid. Steaming after pan-frying ensures the filling is cooked through without sacrificing the sear.

elevations.title: Tare Finish — Concentrated Flavor Bomb at the Bottom
elevations.instruction: In each serving bowl (before adding noodles or broth), whisk together: 1 tablespoon soy sauce, 1 teaspoon toasted sesame oil, 1/2 teaspoon rice vinegar, 1/4 teaspoon grated fresh ginger, and a pinch of white pepper. This is your tare — the concentrated seasoning base that ramen shops use to build depth. Pour the hot dashi over this mixture. The heat blooms the ginger and sesame into the broth instantly. As you eat deeper into the bowl, the flavor intensifies because the tare settles.
elevations.why: Japanese noodle shops don't season the broth uniformly — they build it in layers. The tare at the bottom is more concentrated than what's on top, creating a flavor journey from first sip to last. The fresh ginger and sesame oil in the tare add aromatics that would cook out if simmered in the broth, so adding them raw preserves their punch.

elevations.title: Soft-Boiled Egg and Scallion Forest
elevations.instruction: Bring water to a rolling boil. Lower eggs straight from the refrigerator into the water with a slotted spoon. Set a timer for exactly 6 minutes and 45 seconds. Transfer immediately to an ice bath for 5 full minutes. Peel under running water. Halve and nestle into the bowl yolk-side up. The yolk should be jammy — set at the edges, molten gold in the center. For the scallion forest: slice 4 scallions on a sharp bias into 2-inch pieces. Stand them upright in the bowl, leaning against the egg and dumplings. Add a pinch of togarashi (Japanese seven-spice) over everything.
elevations.why: A soft-boiled egg in soup is a built-in sauce — when you break it, the warm yolk ribbons into the broth and enriches every spoonful it touches. The scallions served tall and raw provide a sharp, oniony crunch that contrasts the soft noodles and silky broth. Togarashi adds a complex heat — chili, citrus, sesame, ginger — in a single sprinkle.

elevations.title: Squeeze the Filling Bone-Dry
elevations.instruction: The number one reason Reuben egg rolls turn soggy is wet sauerkraut (or pickles for Elsie's portion — swap dill pickle spears sliced thin for the kraut, same technique applies). Wrap your sauerkraut or pickles in a clean kitchen towel and wring until not a single drop of moisture falls. Then spread the squeezed filling on a sheet pan and let it air-dry for 10 minutes while you prep the wrappers. Mix the dried sauerkraut or pickles with shredded corned beef, shredded Swiss cheese, and 1 tablespoon of whole-grain mustard per cup of filling. Keep the filling cold — warm filling melts the cheese and weakens the wrappers before they hit the oil.
elevations.why: Moisture is the mortal enemy of a crispy egg roll. Every drop of water in that filling turns to steam during frying, which softens the wrapper from the inside out. The mustard replaces Russian dressing inside the roll (dressing goes on the side for dipping) and adds a sharp bite that cuts through the melted Swiss.

elevations.title: Double-Fry for Shatteringly Crisp Skin
elevations.instruction: Heat 2 inches of canola oil to 325°F. Fry the egg rolls for 2 minutes at this lower temperature — they'll be pale and blonde, not brown. Pull them out, drain on a wire rack, and let them rest for 3 minutes. Now crank the oil to 375°F and fry again for 90 seconds until the skin is deep gold and covered in micro-blisters. This double-fry technique — stolen from French fry methodology — gives you a shell that stays crispy for 15 minutes instead of 3.
elevations.why: The first fry cooks the wrapper through and begins dehydrating the surface. The rest period lets internal moisture migrate outward. The second high-heat fry vaporizes that surface moisture and creates a glass-like crust. This is the same principle that makes Belgian frites and Korean fried chicken supernaturally crunchy.

elevations.title: Homemade Russian Dressing for Dipping
elevations.instruction: Mix 1/2 cup mayonnaise with 2 tablespoons ketchup, 1 tablespoon prepared horseradish, 1 tablespoon pickle relish, 1 teaspoon Worcestershire sauce, 1/2 teaspoon smoked paprika, and a squeeze of lemon juice. Let it sit in the fridge for 20 minutes. Serve in small ramekins alongside the egg rolls. This dressing is the glue that connects the egg roll concept back to its Reuben sandwich roots — without it, you just have a corned beef spring roll.
elevations.why: Store-bought Russian dressing is sweet and flat. Homemade gives you control over the balance of acid, sweetness, heat, and smoke. The horseradish provides the same sinus-clearing punch as the original sandwich, and the smoked paprika adds warmth that bridges the fried wrapper to the deli filling.

elevations.title: Whip the Ricotta Until It's Cloud-Light
elevations.instruction: Put 1 cup of whole-milk ricotta in a food processor with 1 tablespoon of extra-virgin olive oil, the zest of half a lemon, and a generous pinch of salt. Process for a full 2 minutes — not 30 seconds, not 1 minute, 2 minutes — until it transforms from grainy curds into a mousse-like cream that holds soft peaks when you lift the blade. This is the foundation of the crostini, and its texture should be closer to whipped cream than cheese. Chill until assembly.
elevations.why: Most home cooks spread ricotta straight from the tub, and it tastes like ricotta from the tub. Two minutes of processing incorporates air and emulsifies the fats, creating a fundamentally different texture that melts on the tongue instead of sitting there. The lemon zest blooms during processing, perfuming the entire batch.

elevations.title: Smashed Pea Salsa Verde
elevations.instruction: Blanch 1 cup of peas (fresh or frozen) in boiling salted water for exactly 90 seconds, then shock in ice water. Drain and roughly smash with a fork — you want some whole peas and some crushed, not a purée. Fold in 2 tablespoons of chopped fresh mint, 1 tablespoon of chopped fresh chives, 1 tablespoon of olive oil, the juice of half a lemon, and a pinch of flaky salt. The mix should be chunky, bright green, and slightly loose. Spoon over the whipped ricotta on each crostini.
elevations.why: Keeping the pea mixture textured instead of puréed gives you two experiences in one bite: the silky ricotta base and the pop of whole peas with their sweet, starchy burst. Mint is the classic Italian spring pairing with peas — it makes them taste more like themselves, not different.

elevations.title: Garlic-Rubbed Crostini with Flaky Salt Finish
elevations.instruction: Slice a baguette on a sharp bias into 1/2-inch thick ovals. Brush both sides with olive oil and toast on a sheet pan at 400°F for 8-10 minutes until golden and firm but not rock-hard — you want crunch on the outside and a slight chew in the center. While still hot, rub one side of each crostini with a halved raw garlic clove. The rough, toasted surface acts like a Microplane, grating garlic into the bread. Assemble immediately: ricotta, pea mixture, a thread of olive oil, and 3 flakes of Maldon salt.
elevations.why: The garlic-rub technique is Italian bruschetta 101, and it's better than mixing garlic into the toppings because the raw garlic hits your palate first with a sharp, bright heat that the ricotta and peas then cool and soften. The flaky salt on top provides crunch and bursts of salinity that make each bite dynamic.

elevations.title: Build the Dressing in a Blender, Not a Bowl
elevations.instruction: In a blender, combine 1 ripe avocado, 1/2 cup buttermilk, 1/4 cup packed fresh basil, 1/4 cup packed fresh parsley, 2 tablespoons fresh chives, 1 tablespoon fresh tarragon (the signature herb — don't skip it), 1 clove raw garlic, the juice of 1 lemon, 2 tablespoons olive oil, 1 tablespoon rice vinegar, and salt. Blend until completely smooth and vibrant green — about 45 seconds. Taste aggressively: it should be tangy, herby, and slightly garlicky. If it's flat, it needs more salt and lemon. Thin with buttermilk if needed to a pourable consistency.
elevations.why: Green Goddess dressing gets its name from a 1920s San Francisco recipe that was herb-forward and creamy. The avocado adds body and fat without dairy heaviness, and the blender fully breaks down the herbs into a smooth emulsion that coats every leaf uniformly. Tarragon is the herb that makes Green Goddess taste like Green Goddess — without it, it's just ranch in a green dress.

elevations.title: Charred Snap Peas for the Crunch Layer
elevations.instruction: Toss 1 cup of sugar snap peas with 1 tablespoon olive oil and a pinch of salt. Sear in a dry cast-iron skillet over high heat for 2 minutes, shaking once. You want black blisters on the pods but the interior still crisp and raw. Slice on a sharp bias and scatter over the dressed salad alongside thinly sliced radishes and toasted sunflower seeds.
elevations.why: A salad without textural contrast is just wet leaves. Charred snap peas give you three textures in one ingredient: the blistered exterior, the snappy pod, and the sweet pea inside. Cutting on the bias exposes more interior surface area and looks beautiful against the green dressing.

elevations.title: Crispy Shallot Rings
elevations.instruction: Slice 2 shallots into thin rings, separate them, and toss with 1 tablespoon of cornstarch and a pinch of salt. Fry in 1/2 inch of canola oil at 325°F, stirring gently, until deep amber — about 4-5 minutes. Pull them before you think they're done; residual heat carries them the rest of the way. Drain on a wire rack. Scatter over the salad at the last possible moment — these lose their crunch within 5 minutes of hitting the dressing.
elevations.why: Crispy shallots are the universal salad upgrade that transforms a side dish into something people fight over. The cornstarch creates a micro-coating that crisps faster and stays crunchy longer. On a wire rack, air circulates underneath and prevents steam from softening the bottom — paper towels trap moisture.

elevations.title: Za'atar Pita Chips — Baked Until Shattered
elevations.instruction: Split 2 pita breads into their two layers (this is critical — you want thin, single-layer pieces for maximum crispness). Tear into rough 1-inch shards. Toss with 2 tablespoons of olive oil, 1 tablespoon of za'atar, and a pinch of flaky salt. Spread in a single layer on a sheet pan and bake at 400°F for 8-10 minutes until deeply golden and rigid — they should shatter when you snap one. Cool completely before adding to the salad. Add them at the very last second before serving.
elevations.why: Fattoush lives or dies by its bread. Split pita crisps faster and more evenly than whole pita. The za'atar's dried thyme and sumac bloom in the oven heat, becoming intensely aromatic. Adding the chips last is non-negotiable — soggy pita is just wet bread, and wet bread has no business on a plate.

elevations.title: Pomegranate-Sumac Dressing
elevations.instruction: Whisk together 3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, 2 tablespoons fresh lemon juice, 1 tablespoon pomegranate molasses, 1 clove grated garlic, 1 teaspoon ground sumac, and salt to taste. The dressing should taste sharp, slightly sweet, and almost tingly from the sumac. Dress the salad vegetables 5 minutes before serving so they absorb some dressing, but add the pita chips dry and undressed at the last second.
elevations.why: Pomegranate molasses is the secret ingredient that separates a great fattoush from a good one. It adds a tart, fruity depth that straight lemon juice can't match. Sumac doubles down on the citrusy tang without adding liquid. Dressing the vegetables ahead lets the tomatoes and cucumbers release their juices into the vinaigrette, creating a natural flavor pool at the bottom of the bowl.

elevations.title: Chunk Everything Large and Rustic
elevations.instruction: Cut your tomatoes into thick wedges, not dice. Slice cucumbers into half-moons 1/4-inch thick. Tear romaine leaves by hand into 2-inch pieces. Slice radishes into coins. Everything should be big enough to stab with a fork and identify. Add a generous handful of torn fresh mint and flat-leaf parsley — not chopped, torn. The herbs should be visible, not invisible.
elevations.why: Fattoush is a peasant salad — its beauty is in its rusticity. Small dice makes it look like pico de gallo. Large, irregular pieces create varying textures in every bite and show off the ingredients' natural colors. Torn herbs release more aromatic oil from their broken cells than a clean knife cut.

elevations.title: Mandoline-Thin Ribbons, Not Shreds
elevations.instruction: Run your carrots and radishes lengthwise down a mandoline set to paper-thin — you should almost see through them. If you don't have a mandoline, use a Y-peeler on the carrots to create long, wide ribbons and slice radishes as thin as humanly possible with a sharp knife. Drop the shaved vegetables into a bowl of ice water for 10 minutes — they'll curl into elegant spirals as they chill and crisp. Drain and spin dry before dressing.
elevations.why: Thin vegetables have more surface area to catch dressing, so every bite is seasoned. The ice bath crisps the ribbons and triggers a slight curl that adds height and visual drama to the plate. This is a $0 technique upgrade that makes a simple salad look like it came from a restaurant.

elevations.title: Toasted Sesame-Ginger Dressing
elevations.instruction: Whisk together 2 tablespoons toasted sesame oil, 1 tablespoon rice vinegar, 1 tablespoon soy sauce, 1 teaspoon honey, 1 teaspoon freshly grated ginger, and the juice of half a lime. In a dry pan over medium heat, toast 2 tablespoons of sesame seeds until they turn one shade darker and start popping — about 2 minutes. Add half the toasted seeds to the dressing and reserve the rest for garnish. Dress the salad just before serving.
elevations.why: Toasting sesame seeds releases their oil and deepens their flavor from subtle to assertive. Splitting them between the dressing and the garnish gives you two sesame experiences: the dissolved nuttiness in the liquid and the crunchy pops on top. Fresh ginger's heat fades quickly, so grate it at the last minute.

elevations.title: Crispy Wonton Strip Garnish
elevations.instruction: Stack 4 wonton wrappers, cut into 1/4-inch strips with a sharp knife. Separate the strips and fry in 1 inch of canola oil at 350°F for about 45 seconds until golden and puffed. Drain on a wire rack and season with a pinch of salt immediately. Scatter over the dressed salad just before serving for a crispy element that echoes the Asian flavor profile.
elevations.why: This salad is all smooth, thin surfaces — shaved vegetables, liquid dressing. The wonton strips add a shattering crunch that breaks up the textural monotony and ties the dish visually to the Asian flavor palette. They take 2 minutes and transform the salad from a side to a destination.

elevations.title: Warm Honey-Balsamic Vinaigrette
elevations.instruction: In a small saucepan, combine 3 tablespoons balsamic vinegar, 1 tablespoon honey, and a pinch of salt. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 2 minutes until slightly thickened and syrupy. Remove from heat and whisk in 3 tablespoons of extra-virgin olive oil in a thin stream until emulsified. Dress the salad while the vinaigrette is still warm — not hot, warm. The gentle heat wilts the arugula just at the edges, concentrating its peppery bite, while the strawberries soften slightly and release a blush of juice.
elevations.why: A warm vinaigrette on a cool salad creates a temperature contrast that heightens every flavor. The reduced balsamic has a concentrated sweetness and viscosity that clings to leaves instead of pooling at the bottom. It bridges the tart strawberries and the peppery arugula in a way cold dressing cannot.

elevations.title: Candied Pecans with Black Pepper
elevations.instruction: In a dry skillet over medium heat, toss 1/2 cup pecan halves with 1 tablespoon honey, a generous crack of black pepper, and a pinch of flaky salt. Stir constantly for 3-4 minutes until the honey caramelizes and the pecans are fragrant and sticky. Spread on parchment paper immediately — they harden fast. Break into clusters once cool and scatter over the salad.
elevations.why: Candied nuts add sweetness, crunch, and richness that plain toasted nuts don't. The black pepper adds a subtle heat that prevents them from being one-dimensional. Against the creamy goat cheese and tart strawberries, the candied pecans complete a flavor wheel: sweet, salty, sour, bitter (arugula), umami (aged balsamic). All five tastes in one salad.

elevations.title: Cold-Crumbled Goat Cheese with Fresh Thyme
elevations.instruction: Take your goat cheese log straight from the refrigerator — cold goat cheese crumbles cleanly into irregular chunks instead of smearing. Use your fingers, not a knife, to break it into pea-to-marble-sized pieces over the dressed salad. Finish with a scatter of fresh thyme leaves stripped from the stem. The cold cheese against the warm-dressed greens creates pockets of cool creaminess that change the temperature of every other bite.
elevations.why: Warm vinaigrette + cold cheese = a thermal experience that keeps your palate engaged. Cold goat cheese also holds its shape on the plate rather than melting into the dressing. Fresh thyme adds a woodsy, almost floral note that ties the honey in the dressing to the earthiness of the arugula — it's the hidden thread that makes this salad feel cohesive.
